raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|worth|6984|worthy}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|Ther william was & his ''worth'' burde [wife].
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2522.}}}}
{{smaller block|The more that a man con, the more ''worth'' he ys.
{{right|''Rob. of Gloucester'', p. 364.}}}}
{{smaller block|He . . . accounts himselfe both a fit person to do the noblest and godliest deeds, and much better ''worth'' then to deject and defile with such a debasement and such a pollution as sin is, himselfe so highly ransom’d.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii. 3.}}}}

'''2.''' Having worth, esteem, or value in a given degree; representing a relative or comparative worth (of): used generally with a noun of measurement dependent directly upon it without a preposition.
{{smaller block|A byrd in hand, as some men say, is ''worth'' ten flye at large.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 98.}}}}
{{smaller block|Specifically—(''a'') Having a specified value in money or exchange; representing under fair conditions a price or cost (of); equivalent in value to: expressing either actual market value, or value obtainable under favorable or just conditions.}}
{{smaller block|Schal no deuel at his deth-day deren him ''worth'' a myte.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), viii. 54.}}}}
{{smaller block|A score of good ewes may be ''worth'' ten pounds.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 2. 57.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''b'') Possessed of; having estate to the value of; possessing: as, a man ''worth'' five millions.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To ennoble those
That scarce, some two days since, were ''worth'' a noble.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3. 82.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Poor Rutilus spends all he ’s ''Worth'',
In hopes of setting one good Dinner forth.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Eléventh Satire of Juvenal.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''c'') Having a specified moral value or importance; estimable or esteemed in a given way; reaching a certain grade of excellence.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But I remain’d, whose hopes were dim,</poem> Whose life, whose thoughts, were little ''worth''.
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam.}}}}

'''3.''' Entitled to, by reason of excellence, importance, etc.; meriting; deserving: having the same construction as in sense 2: as, the castle is ''worth'' defending; the matter is not ''worth'' notice.
{{smaller block|Me, wretch more ''worth'' your vengeance.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 1. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|Pray thee, let him alone; he is not ''worth'' thy anger.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|If what one has to say is ''worth'' saying, he need not beg pardon for saying it. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Over the Teacups, xii.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Not worth a continental, a hair, a leek, a maravedi, a rap, a snap,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''The game is not worth the candle.''' See ''candle''.—'''To be worth one’s salt.''' See ''salt''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Worth the whistle.''' See ''whistle''.—'''Worth while.''' See ''while''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''worth'''<sup>2</sup> (wėrth), ''n.''   [< ME. ''worth'', ''werth'', ''wurth'', ''wrth'', also ''worthe'', ''wurthe'', ''werthe'', < AS. ''weorth'', ''wurth'' = OS. ''werth'', ''werd'' = D. ''waarde'' = OHG. ''werd'' (> Lith. ''wertas'', OBulg. ''vredu''?), MHG. ''wert'', G. ''wert'', ''werth'' = Icel. ''verth'' = Sw. ''värde'' = Dan. ''værd'' = Goth. ''wairths'', value; from the adj.: see ''worth''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.'']   '''1†.''' Honor; dignity.
{{smaller block|<poem>I will do what ''worth''
Shall bid me, and no more.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wee read sometimes of two Bishops in one place, and had all the Presbyters there beene of like ''worth'' we might perhaps have read of twenty.
{{right|''Milton'', Prelatical Episcopacy.}}}} '''2.''' Worthiness; excellence of character; excellency; merit; desert: as, a man of great ''worth''.
{{smaller block|<poem>I dispute it not,
His ''worth'' forestals exception.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, iv. 254.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I know your ''worths'',
And thus low bow in reverence to your virtues.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, iii. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Old letters, breathing of her ''worth''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Mariana in the South.}}}}
'''3.''' Value; importance; excellence; valuable or desirable qualities: said of things.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy youth’s proud livery, so gazed on now,
Will be a tatter’d weed, of small ''worth'' held.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|A beautiful object may have a ''worth'' for feeling independent of mere contemplation. {{right|''Mind'', XII. 629.}}}}
'''4.''' Value, especially as expressed in terms of some standard of equivalency or exchange: as, what is his house ''worth''? the ''worth'' of a commodity is usually the price it will bring in market, but price is not always ''worth''.
{{smaller block|<poem>“For ofte haue I,” quod he, “holpe ȝow atte barre,
And ȝit ȝeue ȝe me neuere the ''worthe'' of a russhe.”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), iv. 170.}}}}
{{smaller block|A crown’s ''worth'' of good interpretation.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 2. 99.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If I had but in my pocket
The ''worth'' of one single pennie.</poem>
{{right|''Willie Wallace'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 233).}}}}
'''5.''' That which one is worth; possessions; substance; wealth; riches.
<poem>He that helps him take all my outward ''worth''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 4. 10.}}}}

'''In good worth†''', in good part; without displeasure or offense.
{{smaller block|It becometh me to take it ''in good worth;'' I am not better than he was.
{{right|''Latimer'', 3d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}}
='''Syn. 2''' and '''3.''' ''Merit'', etc. See ''desert''<sup>2</sup>.—'''4.''' ''Value, Cost'', etc. See ''price''.

'''worthful''' (wėrth′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wurthful, worthvolle'', < AS. ''weorthfull'', valuable, < ''weorth'', worth: see ''worth''<sup>2</sup> and ''-ful''.]   Full of worth; worthy.   ''Marston.''
{{smaller block|Those high-born dames and ''worthful'' females whom Margaret the queen had drawn about her.
{{right|''Rock'', Church of our Fathers, ii. 272.}}}}
{{smaller block|Penang and Singapore in the Straits of Malacca, Hong Kong on the route to Canton and Shanghai, are all very ''worthful''.
{{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XL. 373.}}}}

'''worthily''' (wėr′ᴛʜi-li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''worthiliche'', worthily; < ''worthy'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' In a worthy manner; honorably; with due dignity, reverence, or respect; reverently.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Worthili'' hire he wolcomed wen he hire mette.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4290.}}}}
'''2.''' Excellently; rightly; becomingly; suitably; fittingly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou and thy meaner fellows your last service
Did ''worthily'' perform. ''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 36.

He that hath begun so ''worthily'',
It fits not with his resolution
To leave off thus, my lord.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, v. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' Deservedly; justly; according to merit.
{{smaller block|They would not leave their sins, . . . therefore their destruction came ''worthily'' upon them.
{{right|''Latimer'', Sermons and Remains (Parker ed.), p. 51.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Had the gods done so, I had not now
''Worthily'' term’d them merciless to us!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., i. 1. 100.}}}}
{{smaller block|He found out the author, one Dyer, a most crafty fellow and his ancient Maligner, whom he ''worthily'' punished.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 228.}}}}
{{smaller block|You ''worthily'' succeed not only to the honours of your ancestors, but also to their virtues.
{{right|''Dryden'', To the Duke of Ormond, Ded. of Fables.}}}}
{{smaller block|I affirm that some may very ''worthily'' deserve to be hated.
{{right|''South'', Sermons.}}}}

'''worthiness''' (wėr′thi-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''worthinesse, worthynesse''; < ''worthy'', ''a.'', + ''-ness''.]   The quality of being worthy; honor; excellence; dignity; virtue; merit; desert.
{{smaller block|After we shull returne hem for to socoure, for grete pite it were yef thei were deed or taken in so tendre age, for thei ben of high valoure and grete ''worthynesse''.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 197.}}}}
{{smaller block|The prayers which our Saviour made were, for his own ''worthiness'', accepted.
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
{{smaller block|I see, even in her looks, gentry and general ''worthiness''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, ii. 1.}}}}
='''Syn.''' See ''worth''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''

'''worthless''' (wėrth′les), ''a.''   [< ''worth''<sup>2</sup> + ''-less''; < AS. ''wurthleás'', < ''wurth'', worth, + ''-leás'', E. ''-less''.]   '''1.''' Of no value or use; valueless; useless.
{{smaller block|<poem>Silvia is too fair, too true, too holy,
To be corrupted with my ''worthless'' gifts.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 2. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis but a ''worthless'' world to win or lose.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|We read how men sell themselves to a certain Personage, and that Personage cheats them. He gives them wealth; yes, but the gold pieces turn into ''worthless'' leaves.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Roundabout Papers, On a Pear-tree.}}}} '''2.''' Lacking in or destitute of worth, dignity, excellence, or merit; mean; contemptible.
{{smaller block|Some ''worthless'' slave of thine I’ll slay.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 515.}}}}
{{smaller block|Habits of dissimulation and falsehood, no doubt, mark a man of our age and country as utterly ''worthless'' and abandoned.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Machiavelli.}}}}
{{smaller block|The mode of genesis of the worthy and the ''worthless'' seems the same.
{{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychol., I. 552.}}}}
'''3.''' Unworthy; not deserving.
{{smaller block|A peevish schoolboy, ''worthless'' of such honour.
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., v. 1. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Her boons let foolish Fortune throw
On ''worthless'' heads; more glorious ’tis by far
A Diadem to merit than to wear.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, i. 149.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Worthless'' they are of Cæsar’s gracious eyes.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Unserviceable, unprofitable.—'''2.''' Base, vile, depraved, graceless, trashy, trumpery, flimsy, tinsel, trifling, paltry, frivolous.}}

'''worthlessly''' (wėrth′les-li), ''adv.'' In a worthless manner.

'''worthlessness''' (wėrth′les-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being worthless.

'''worthly†''' (wėrth′li), ''a.''   [ME. ''worthely'', ''wurthliche''; < ''worth''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Worthy; excellent.
{{smaller block|<poem>What schulde the mone ther compas clym,
& to euen wyth that ''worthly'' lyȝt
That schynez vpon brokez brym?</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), i. 1071.}}}}
<poem>But onely the ''worthely'' warke of my wyll
In my sprete sall enspyre the mighte of me.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''York Plays'', p. 2.}}}}

'''worthy''' (wėr′ᴛ̵ʜi), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''worthy'', ''worthi'', ''wurthy'', ''wurthi'', worthy (not found in AS.), = OS. ''wirthig'' = MD. ''weerdigh'' = MLG. ''werdig'' = OHG. ''wirdīg'', MHG. ''wirdec'', G. ''würdig'', worthy, = Icel. ''verthugr'' = Sw. ''värdig'' = Dan. ''værdig''; as ''worth''<sup>2</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Having worth; of high standing or degree; honorable; worshipful; excellent; deserving of honor, respect, praise, mention, attention, or the like; valuable; noble; estimable; virtuous; meritorious: noting persons and things.
{{smaller block|Therfore whan the Soudan wille avance ony ''worthi'' Knyghte, he makethe him a Amyralle.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Tho moste ''worthiest'' thes brethren gan take,
Vnto the castel conueing thaim certayn.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1823.}}}}
{{smaller block|Salust is a wise and ''worthy'' writer.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 154.}}}}
{{smaller block|I have done thee ''worthy'' service.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 247.}}}}
{{smaller block|Against him Mauritius performed ''worthie'' attempts, which made way vnto him for the Roman Empire.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 359.}}}}
{{smaller block|A really ''worthy'' life depends not only on the vividness and constancy of the ruling moral idea, but also on its volume and contents.
{{right|''J. Sully'', Sensation and Intuition, p. 148.}}}}
'''2†.''' Of high rank or social station.
{{smaller block|<poem>And though that he were ''worthy'', he was wys,
And of his port as meek as is a mayde.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 68.}}}}

'''3.''' Deserving; meriting: sometimes followed by ''of'' before the thing merited or deserved, sometimes by an accusative directly, and sometimes by an infinitive.
{{smaller block|<poem>ȝe, sire, bote I pertly vndo that I haue the profred,
I am ''worthi'' muche blame; what mai I seiȝe more?</poem>
{{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Now trewly ye be ''worthy to'' haue grete blame, for youre peple haue moche losse hadde seth ye wente from the bataile.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 404.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Worthy'' the owner, and the owner it.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5. 64.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh, thou hast open’d
A book in which, writ down in bloody letters,
My conscience finds that I am ''worthy of''
More than I undergo!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Epaminondas, amongst the Thebans, is ''worthy of'' note and memory, even to our ages and those that shall succeed us.
{{right|''Ford'', Line of Life.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Friends! we have liv’d too long. I never heard
Sounds such as these, so ''worthy to'' be feared.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Needless Alarm.}}}}
{{smaller block|When we consider a right or a wrong action as done by another person, we think of that person as ''worthy of'' moral approbation or reprobation.
{{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, II. 130.}}}}

'''4.''' Well-deserved.
{{smaller block|Doing ''worthy'' vengeance on thyself.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 2. 87.}}}}

'''5.''' In keeping with the standing, character, dignity, etc. (of); fit; fitted; proper; suited; suitable: with ''of'', ''for'', or an infinitive clause.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whan a werkman hath wrouȝte thanne may men se the sothe,</poem>}}
<poem>What he were ''worthi for'' his werke and what he hath de-
serued;
And nouȝt to fonge bifore for drede of disalowynge.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiv. 139.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Worthy for'' an empress’ love.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 4. 76.}}}}

<poem>Wert thou a subject ''worthy of'' my sword,
Or that thy death, this moment, could call home
My banish’d hopes, thou now wert dead; dead, woman!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, v. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|If your parts be ''worthy of'' me, I will countenance you.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, i. 1.}}}}

<poem>White gloves, and linen ''worthy'' Lady Mary!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, I. i. 164.}}}}

{{smaller block|After the greatest consociation of religious duties for preparation, no man can be sufficiently ''worthy to'' communicate.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 313.}}}}

{{smaller block|Foemen ''worthy of'' their steel.
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., v. 10.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Worthiest of blood''', in ''law'', a phrase applied to males, as opposed to females, in the succession to inheritance. See ''tanistry''.}}

'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''worthies'' (-ᴛ̵ʜiz). '''1.''' A person of eminent worth; one distinguished for serviceable and estimable qualities: as, Fuller’s “History of the ''Worthies'' of England.”

<poem>Thou thyselfe dost now repute
The wort[h]iest ''wort[h]y'' of the race of Brute.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 26.}}}}

<poem>What do these ''worthies''
But rob and spoil, burn, slaughter, and enslave
Peaceable nations?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iii. 74.}}}}

{{smaller block|At the first appearance of my work, its aim and drift were misapprehended by some of the descendants of the Dutch ''worthies''.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 13.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
